sections.h2: Which offices handle property tax in Calhoun County?
sections.html:
Property tax in Calhoun County is split between local assessors, the county treasurer and a local board of review. The County Treasurer's Office, at 315 West Green Street in Marshall, collects delinquent real estate taxes, keeps the books on collections for the county's 28 townships, cities and villages, and runs the delinquent tax reversion process of title searches, court hearings, foreclosure and auction. It also issues deed certifications and takes part in the Calhoun County Land Bank.

  • General questions, delinquent taxes, hardship extensions and deed certification: 269-781-0807.
  • Homestead and taxable value changes: 269-781-0808.
  • Land bank questions: 269-781-0777.
  • Hours: Monday through Thursday 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Friday 8 a.m. to noon.

Your city or township assessor sets the value on the parcel, so questions about a specific assessment start there. Ask the treasurer or your local unit for the millage rates on your own bill.

sections.h2: How is a Calhoun County home assessed and taxed?
sections.html:
Michigan assesses property at 50% of true cash value, and each year's taxable value is the lesser of the prior year's taxable value times 1.05 or the inflation rate, or the current state equalized value, according to MCL 211.27a. A transfer of ownership resets taxable value to the state equalized value for the following year.

That reset matters to anyone selling in Calhoun County. A house whose taxable value has been held down by the cap for years can see a noticeably higher bill once the buyer takes title. For scale, the Census median owner-occupied value in the county is $162,800, which at a 50% assessment ratio would put a median house near $81,400 of state equalized value.

Tell a buyer the new owner's bill may rise after the transfer, and point them to the treasurer's taxable value line at 269-781-0808 if they want to ask before closing.

sections.h2: When are Calhoun County property taxes due and appealed?
sections.html:
The calendar below is set by state statute and repeats each year, so it applies to Calhoun County bills as it does anywhere in Michigan.

Recurring Michigan property tax dates that apply in Calhoun County (statute cited in each row)
StepRuleSource
Board of reviewMeets the second Monday in March, at least 12 hours that weekMCL 211.30
Principal residence exemptionAffidavit filed by June 1 for the summer bill or November 1 for the winter billMCL 211.7cc
Summer taxLien and due July 1; interest added after September 14MCL 211.44a
Tax Tribunal, residentialPetition by July 31 of the tax yearMCL 205.735a
Fee windowUp to 1% fee through February 14; a 3% late charge may followMCL 211.44
DelinquencyUnpaid summer taxes are returned delinquent on March 1MCL 211.44a

Commercial and industrial petitions to the tribunal are due May 31 instead of July 31.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Calhoun County assessment?
sections.html:
Start with the local board of review in March. A residential owner must protest there before the Michigan Tax Tribunal will take the case, and the board must give written notice of its decision, with appeal rights, by the first Monday in June. A taxpayer who lives outside the area may send the protest and supporting papers by letter, so no personal appearance is needed.

If the board does not fix the value, the next step is a written petition to the Tax Tribunal, mailed or delivered by July 31 for residential and farm property. A petition counts as filed when it is postmarked, hand delivered or handed to a designated delivery service by the deadline. The petition also has to be served on the local assessor by certified mail. An owner may appear personally or hire an attorney or another representative.

Disputes over a denied principal residence exemption go to the July or December board of review first. The statutes are MCL 211.30 and MCL 205.735a.

sections.h2: What help does Calhoun County offer when taxes fall behind?
sections.html:
The treasurer offers a financial hardship extension for owner-occupied homes. It delays the foreclosure deadline by up to one year for homeowners who are working to catch up on forfeited taxes, and it requires a payment plan. Interest of 1.5% a month, fees and penalties keep accruing during the extension, so the total owed still grows. The application is online, and the office sets an appointment after receiving the paperwork and documents. Call 269-781-0807.

  • Disabled veterans exemption: for an honorably discharged Michigan resident rated permanently and totally disabled by the VA at the 100% rate, or with a VA certificate for specially adapted housing, or rated individually unemployable. The surviving spouse can qualify. File the State Tax Commission affidavit with the local assessor every year.
  • Principal residence exemption: an affidavit filed with the local tax collecting unit under MCL 211.7cc.
  • Foreclosure auctions: the county publishes results for 2013 through 2025 in its document center, a useful record of what tax-foreclosed parcels have sold for.

For taxes that have gone through foreclosure, ask the treasurer about the reversion timeline before the auction date is set.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid taxes when you sell a Calhoun County house?
sections.html:
Unpaid taxes are a lien on the property and follow it into the sale. Summer taxes become a lien and are due on July 1, and after the last payable day a county fee of 4% plus interest at 1% a month attaches to amounts collected late, under MCL 211.44. Once taxes are returned delinquent on March 1 they move to the county treasurer's collection process.

A warranty deed cannot be recorded until the county treasurer certifies that no tax liens or titles are held and that five years of taxes are paid, per MCL 211.135. The Register of Deeds charges $5 for that certification. Plan to clear any balance with the title company so the certificate issues before the closing date.

sections.h2: What is Calhoun County like for a property owner?
sections.html:
Calhoun County has 706 square miles of land, a 2025 population of 133,408 and a population density of 190.2 people per square mile. Population slipped 0.7% between the April 2020 base and July 2025. Battle Creek is the largest city and Marshall is the seat.

About 20.2% of residents are 65 or older, 14.5% live in poverty, the average commute is 20.5 minutes and the county recorded 120 building permits in 2025. Retail sales ran $16,721 per resident in 2022, far above Cass County's $6,832. Median selected monthly owner costs are $1,271 with a mortgage and $545 without one.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Calhoun County, Michigan?
faqs.a: Your city or township treasurer collects the regular bill, and the County Treasurer collects taxes returned as delinquent. The county treasurer's number is 269-781-0807 at 315 West Green Street in Marshall.

faqs.q: When is the Calhoun County board of review?
faqs.a: It meets on the second Monday in March, or on the Tuesday or Wednesday after if the local unit chooses, and sits at least 12 hours that week. Contact your assessor for the exact local schedule.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal to the Michigan Tax Tribunal?
faqs.a: July 31 of the tax year for residential, agricultural and timber-cutover real property, and May 31 for commercial, industrial and developmental property. Residential owners must protest at the board of review first.

faqs.q: Can Calhoun County delay a tax foreclosure?
faqs.a: Yes, for owner-occupied homes. A financial hardship extension can delay the foreclosure deadline up to one year when the owner sets up a payment plan, though 1.5% monthly interest and fees keep accruing.

faqs.q: Do I pay property tax at closing in Calhoun County?
faqs.a: Any balance due is normally settled at closing through the title company. A warranty deed needs a county treasurer certification of paid taxes first, and the Register of Deeds charges $5 for it.
